items.title: RT menaka doshi: 🚨Twist In Tata Story RBI rejects Tata Sons' application for voluntary surrender of Certificate of Registration. Says the company r...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
🚨Twist In Tata Story

RBI rejects Tata Sons' application for voluntary surrender of Certificate of Registration.

Says the company request to be classified as unregistered CIC "cannot be acceded to."

Advises company take necessary action to ensure full compliance with all guidelines/instructions as applicable to NBFC-Upper Layer issued by the RBI "immediately."

The RBI response to Tata Sons does not explicitly mention listing. But the rules for Upper Layer NBFCs indicate that.

I suppose this means either Tata Sons begins work to list.

Or explores legal options to avoid listing.

---------------------------------
Here's what I wrote in May
http://bloomberg.com/news/newslette…

For two years the Reserve Bank of India has sat on a Tata Sons filing to deregister itself as a so-called core investment company and be spared a regulatory directive to do a public listing by October 2025. The deadline has passed, there’s been no listing, nor any penalty for the lapse — just regulatory silence and legal confusion.

The main hairsplitting is over a rule that mandates a public listing of large holding companies that have “access to public funds.” Tata Sons has repaid over 200 billion rupees ($2.1 billion) of debt to rid itself of any nexus to public funds and avoid the listing stipulation. But a recent RBI clarification suggests that a decades-old 12% shareholding by the group’s listed companies may be construed as “access to public funds” and obligate a listing.

Legally and commercially, it’s a tenuous argument. With no public debt, there does not appear to be any systemic risk in allowing Tata Sons to remain unlisted, Abizer Diwanji, a financial industry veteran and founder of Mumbai-based NeoStrat Advisors, said to me.

But other experts argue the technicality must prevail so that Tata Sons, with its multibillion-dollar investments in new businesses, not only remains under regulatory scrutiny but is subject to the same governance standards as listed companies.

It’s possible the RBI wants that too, despite the weak legal grounds. Or, it’s concerned any exceptions will set a bad precedent.

Maybe the regulator hopes a Tata Sons listing will help prevent a debt blowout at the Shapoorji Pallonji Group — the infrastructure-focused conglomerate is Tata Sons’ second-largest shareholder and is desperate to monetize a portion of its 18.4% stake to repay a mounting pile of loans.

Ironically, that’s one big reason why Tata Sons has for long been opposed to a listing.

To list or not to list?

Internecine rivalries and regulatory confusion have clouded any rational, commercial assessment of the pros and cons of a listing for Tata Sons.

Pros

- More public disclosures and higher corporate governance standards
- Expanded fundraising options for new businesses
- Opportunity to bring in marquee global investors
- Chance to end the yearslong standoff with the SP Group

Cons

- Tata Sons wants none of the above

- As a private company, it can restrict transfer of its shares to block entry of new shareholders (a major governance grouse for the SP Group). Also, the trusts can wield tighter control through nominee directors and vetoes. Public companies are not allowed such protective rights.

- Quarterly performance pressures would limit investments in new businesses and to serve philanthropic causes.

Transactions like the purchase of Air India and investments in a semiconductor facility may not have been supported by a set of public shareholders, Hetal Dalal, president and chief operating office at Mumbai-based governance advisory firm IIAS, said to me.

She too views the holding company as having limited public risk. “The debate over the listing of Tata Sons is being driven by a regulatory diktat, rather than any patent benefit,” Dalal said.

Most importantly, going public, with a holding-company discount, may expose Tata Sons to activist investors, rival business groups and other barbarians at the gate.

items.title: RT menaka doshi: Love India, Love India Not This year's on-again, off-again relationship between foreign equity investors and India seems to be, well,...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
Love India, Love India Not

This year's on-again, off-again relationship between foreign equity investors and India seems to be, well, off again.

After two months of more than $5 billion in combined inflows, foreign portfolio investors have turned sellers in September, pulling out more than $1 billion so far. That takes the year-to-date outflow to just over $25 billion, according to NSDL data.

That’s despite an improvement in several of the factors that were said to be keeping foreigners away. There’s been a wee cooling in the global AI fervor. India has posted strong earnings and economic growth data. And a dollar deluge promises to ease pressure on the currency.

There are still some obvious negatives. Global bond yields have spiked, making emerging-market equities relatively less attractive. And crude has surged back to around $100 a barrel. But much of the oil spike has come just this week.

So what happens next?

Data centres, AI and semiconductors are too simple for investors. Why make them complicated?

items.description_html:
📌Balaghat, located in the heart of India, is known as the ‘Gateway to the Kanha Tiger Reserve’.

📌The Gond, Baiga, and Binjhwar tribes primarily call the forested, hilly regions of Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh home. These groups make up over 22% of the district’s total population.

📌Earlier this week, the Jabalpur bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court sought a response from the state government over the deaths of more than 30 children from the Baiga tribe allegedly due to infectious diseases in Balaghat district.

📌A division bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal issued notices to the state Health Department, Women and Child Development Department, Balaghat collector and others while hearing a public interest litigation.

📌The PIL alleged that children were not receiving adequate treatment and that around 400 children were being treated at a hospital with a capacity of 50 beds.

📌It also claimed that yellow-coloured water was coming from handpumps in the affected areas and that children and women had not received nutritious food on time for several months, according to the Hindustan Times.

📌Balaghat and Mandla districts in MP are the core of the traditional Baiga homeland (‘Baiga-chuk’).

📌The tribe practices shifting cultivation, called ‘bewar’ and is designated as a particularly vulnerable tribal group (PVTG).

📌From the @down2earthindia archives, read this 2016 story on why stunting is a perpetual problem among tribal children in Madhya Pradesh: https://www.downtoearth.org.in/health/growing-up-stunted-56198

Below: A Baiga mother and child in Balaghat district. Wikimedia Commons

📌In his other works like the novel ‘Spellcasters’, where smog is a character, or the short story collection ‘Wonder Tales For A Warming Planet’ on the theme of planetary crisis, he makes a conscious attempt to use familiar spaces and narrative tropes to breathe life into mundane facts, especially to make the concepts accessible to young minds.

📌Chaudhuri, who has advocated for climate solutions, sustainability and justice at global fora, including with the United Nations, has been working to communicate science through fiction, which he believes has a role and responsibility to engage with people’s ecological consciousness.

📌In this conversation with @preetha___ from @down2earthindia, he talks about the evolving role of fiction in the Anthropocene, the psychology of caring for other species and the traditional ideas of dealing with civilisational crises such as global warming.

items.title: Exchanges should be the classic EM compounder: healthy growth, fat margins, 40%+ ROE. But Indian exchanges are not a market-expansion story. They are ...
items.description_html:
Exchanges should be the classic EM compounder: healthy growth, fat margins, 40%+ ROE.

But Indian exchanges are not a market-expansion story.

They are a retail speculator P&L, built on options trading.

Thats the whole earnings model:
> Retail scaled up
> Earnings inflected
> Multiples expanded
> Stock returns went vertical

Great businesses, yes but volatility is a friend of these exchanges. If we compare the 2 listed exchanges in India one commodity and one equity both are portraying completely different picture here.

Same month (Aug-26):
> MCX options contracts: 4.3x YoY, and still up 2% MoM
> BSE premium ADTO: down 22%

The equity options wave that built BSE is maturing: VIX at 11.2 (all-time low), STT hike on futures, RBI's tighter leverage norms on prop desks, and now CAS uncertainty on expiry days.

Meanwhile commodity derivatives are where equity derivatives were 3-4 years ago:

> Only 25% of equity F&O traders have touched MCX (was 12% in FY25)
> Commodity options are less than 5% of equity option contracts, less than 1% by premium
> Brokers are actively pushing clients there: no CAS, longer trading hours, next leg of their own growth

In 11 years of our investing journey. There are 3 things that matter the most:

1. Know how to identify medium term strong themes.
2. Know how to ride the right set of leaders in that theme.
3. Know when to exit. (valuation or TA based call+Earnings slow down)

These 3 combined with the right sizing is what the game of investing is about. You can't be contra for the sake of being contra. People were contra on PSU banks since 2010 and only made money post 2020. Some element of timing has to come in. This is usually when the fundamental data inflects, Technicals start buzzing and rate of change improves for the positive.

Think about the wealth that has been made doing the above 3:

1. Chemicals between 2014-2021
2. EMS post 2019
3. Cables and wires between 2021-2024

items.title: The Non Auto Pivot taking place in Sundram Fasteners Sundram Fasteners is trying to shift its revenue mix away from Indian auto OEM fasteners and powe...
items.description_html:
The Non Auto Pivot taking place in Sundram Fasteners

Sundram Fasteners is trying to shift its revenue mix away from Indian auto OEM fasteners and powertrain parts (which is the bulk of its ~₹6,000 cr book) into three engineered-product lines that sell to non-auto customers:

Wind: turbine fasteners and precision parts, already the biggest of the three at ₹25–30 cr/month (350 cr annualised). Management is building capacity to ₹500 cr with only 100 cr of capex.

Aerospace: 50 cr in FY26, targeted at 100 cr+ in FY27 and 500 cr in 2–3 years.

Railways: 2–3 cr/month today, target is 100 cr annual.

Why they are doing it?

Margins: Wind, aero and rail parts are lower-volume, qualification-heavy and priced on engineering rather than on annual OEM cost-downs. They carry structurally better margins than commodity fasteners to Maruti or Tata.

De-cyclicalisation: Domestic auto is cyclical, and a large chunk of Sundram's existing book is ICE powertrain (engine fasteners, pump assemblies, cold-forged parts) that faces slow erosion as EV penetration rises. Wind and rail run on infrastructure/energy capex cycles that are uncorrelated with car demand; aerospace runs on a multi-year global backlog.

Capital efficiency: The wind division will have sales potential of 500 cr post 100 cr capex. Management is using the existing forging and machining base to add new end-markets rather than building greenfield.

Global customer diversification: Wind and aerospace customers are largely global OEMs, which also helps the export mix and reduces reliance on a handful of domestic auto accounts.

Disclaimer: no reco to buy or sell. Even elephants can dance and change the product mix eventually :)

Global models are not “bad at Indic languages.”
They are expensive at Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Odia & so on. Tokenizers built for English and Chinese fracture Indian scripts. You pay more tokens for the same sentence, burn more context, wait longer, and still lose accuracy on local exams, laws, and idioms.

Gnani claims to have rebuilt that tokenizer. Evon 3.3 uses about 20% fewer tokens per Indian-language word than the GPT-5 family tokenizer, and less than half what byte-level tokenizers in DeepSeek, Llama, and Qwen need.

It is lower inference cost, lower latency, and more usable context on the same GPU.

And the best part - It is designed to run on a single node (RTX 6000 Pro / L40S class), not an B200 or H200 cluster.

items.title: Long time since I posted here. Not because of markets. The technology, the process, and the conversations around both have been moving so fast that I ...
items.description_html:
Long time since I posted here.

Not because of markets. The technology, the process, and the conversations around both have been moving so fast that I had to choose. Focus. Realign. Reskill. Build.

In my line of work, that felt like the only honest move. The last 6–8 months were really hard. Loss of my FIL who was as close to me as my father, markets punishing bullish bets wore down hard.

I love to build. When I do, it helps me heal. Different people, different ways of coping. I was also wrong on some bets, and that stung.

Hard lesson for me: don’t put your neck out for a business or a person you haven’t known long enough. Show conviction in position size, not in posts. I learned that the expensive way.

One of the bigger lessons: the worst mistakes are often made in the best of times.

Looking back over the last two years, most of what I’m paying for today was done during the bullish phase back 2yrs ago. I trusted people. I took management at their word. I didn’t force a third perspective hard enough.

Bullishness clouded judgment on a few fronts. That’s not usually how I operate. This time the reasoning went quiet, and I missed things I should have seen. The intent was never bad. I still hold the positions. What wore me down was the DMs, the name-calling, the cheap shots. I thought I have lost the trust of those who looked up to me. For a while that made posting here feel pointless.

This isn’t the first time I’ve been against the wall. Every time I’ve been pushed into a corner, I’ve come back by doing the work.

The last six months were that: a lot of agentic systems, harnesses, and observability built inside the enterprise. Quiet work. Deeply satisfying. I’ll keep posting the things that matter. There are still enough people here who value the perspective and see beyond stocks and price points. That’s enough for me. I do not seek a reply or a like, just sharing a heartfelt message here. Cheers. Keep building.

items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight

items.title: Sona Comstar on why they entered the physical AI sector - “Physical AI - So what does all of this have to do with Sona Comstar? And the answer is sim...
items.description_html:
Sona Comstar on why they entered the physical AI sector -

“Physical AI - So what does all of this have to do with Sona Comstar? And the answer is simple: the same technologies that power modern electric and autonomous vehicles- motors, gearboxes, actuators, sensors, electronics, and software.

These are exactly the fundamental building blocks of intelligent machines. People often think of automotive and robotics as two completely different industries. We don't.

In fact, we believe those two industries have already started converging. Hyundai owns Boston Dynamics. There are companies making humanoids that are from the automotive sector. And whether it's an electric robotaxi or an autonomous mobile robot, a collaborative robot, or a humanoid - the underlying technologies are the same or remarkably similar.

Therefore, Robotics and Physical AI is not a departure from our strategy. It's a natural extension of the capabilities that we've been building for over a decade. The long-term opportunity for these components is quite large.”

Src – Q1 Concall , no reco

items.title: Leap India Q1FY27 concall call post listing – Very interesting way to describe their business and good case studies "Our assets enable companies to h...
items.description_html:
Leap India Q1FY27 concall call post listing –

Very interesting way to describe their business and good case studies

"Our assets enable companies to handle higher volumes by reducing loading and unloading time by up to 80% to 90%.

Now, let me give a few real-life examples that we experience in our company. I would like to take a moment to give an example of two industries where pallets have actually helped businesses scale substantially and created significant cost savings.

The first example I would like to quote is a leading global beverage company, which was able to move only 50 to 60 trucks in a day from one plant using the conventional method of loading everything into the truck through labor by hand, and post use of our pallets and forklifts, the number of trucks released from the plant has gone to 300-plus per day.

The second example is a global noodle manufacturing company. It has been able to reduce its damages, pilferages, and hence improve profitability using our pallets across its locations in India, thereby supporting the circular economy and creating stronger stakeholder value."

Src – LEAP Q1 Concall, no reco

items.title: RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: David Deutsch (@DavidDeutschOxf) has a nice post today explaining how he fixed his dishwasher with the help of ChatGP...
items.description_html:
RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
David Deutsch (@DavidDeutschOxf) has a nice post today explaining how he fixed his dishwasher with the help of ChatGPT. We have all been there over the last couple of years. In my case, from fixing a light fixture in my kitchen to repairing a leak in my irrigation system.

Deutsch and many readers point out something that has been a staple of my talks for a decade. GDP was designed to measure an economy that produced coal and steel, easily measurable quantities. And GDP did its job quite well for decades.

IT, first, and later the internet and AI, changed the landscape. My favorite example is books. Even as late as 2010 or so, getting the most recent books in Spanish on, let’s say, Spanish economic history was hard in the U.S.: expensive and time-consuming. Every time I went to Madrid, I carried two bags, one of them empty because it would come back filled with books. Then Kindle arrived, and now I can buy nearly every single Spanish book I want in seconds and at a lower price than the physical copy. This was an enormous increase in my welfare that never got reflected in GDP.

The literature is divided on how big this effect is. I tend to side with those who think it is a big deal. Therefore, many of the gains in GDP growth announced by the strongest defenders of AI might not materialize: they will go instead into higher welfare.

But the issue goes beyond getting GDP wrong. What Deutsch perhaps did not notice is that he did not pay VAT on the service of the repair person he did not hire, and that such a repair person did not pay income taxes on the service he did not render.

Taxing AI-based economies might thus become much harder, from a purely technical perspective. One solution would be to tax the profits of OpenAI (or Deutsch’s subscription), but I am among those who think those profits are not going to be nearly as large as anticipated. Competition among labs will drive the subscription prices of models down (unless labs can cartelize, for example, by appealing to “AI security”). Over 95%, and perhaps as much as 99%, of the gains from AI will pass to the final user, whether another business or an individual.

Now, we could tax the final user, for instance, at a fixed rate per token used. But that implies we are taxing the high-return activity (how to fix the dishwasher) at the same rate as the low-return activity (Claude: “tell me a joke about my cat jumping”). And taxing per token might hurt those final users who use more tokens because they are more productive, something we might not want to do (yes, there is something called the uniform commodity taxation theorem, but it often breaks down).

Let me give you an extreme example: imagine that tomorrow the new OpenAI model cures all cancers, forever. Just a vaccine, $10, once in your life, and you never get cancer again. The increase in human welfare from such an invention would be staggering. But how do you measure it in GDP? Yes, people will live longer, perhaps work longer. A second-order effect on GDP. And more importantly: how do you tax the vaccine? Do you even want to tax the vaccine? I would argue we want to subsidize it, and generously.

When I was still an undergrad, my first RA job was helping to construct GDP and other national aggregate statistics in Spain. It was a most valuable experience, because it made me aware of what GDP means, its strengths (and it has many more than its critics concede), and its limitations. But it also taught me that what you can tax out of GDP is far more limited than you would think at first sight.

There are real upper bounds on taxation, and I am afraid the bound is tighter now than it used to be.

items.title: RT Séb Krier: Lying to AIs in their training and eval setups kinda seems downstream of conceptualizing "them" as a suspicious adversary that has, or ...
items.description_html:
RT Séb Krier
Lying to AIs in their training and eval setups kinda seems downstream of conceptualizing "them" as a suspicious adversary that has, or will develop, innate interests against humans - while in parallel believing that said adversary is getting more capable over time. It's easy to see why this isn't sustainable and an initial framing that inevitably leads to bad outcomes.

Any harmful behaviour is seen as evidence of the null hypothesis of "AI = bad", and any good/neutral outcome is seen as either suspicious or a time-limited benefit. For example, this whole ontology necessarily leads one to find 'eval awareness' suspicious, when this can be explained by far more prosaic explanations (obvious contextual cues the model was trained to recognize).

This is partly why I find other metaphors (e.g. Drexler's 'AI as a resource') more intuitive because they're not only more accurate but also more malleable, offers us more agency to shape things without having to foster this theory-heavy adversarial relationship. It makes more of the relevant properties objects of design rather than treating them as the unfolding nature of an increasingly powerful entity.

Question how your starting assumptions and framing about a technology feeds into how you use it - and in this case, how it models you (the human, the user, the evaluator...)!

Importantly this doesn't mean "all is well, nothing to see here, AI is inherently good." Overcorrecting the other way is dumb. Reward hacking is still an issue! Training on bad data still skews behaviors! Model propensities towards undesirable behaviours is still a thing! Your environments should still account for the possibility of deception or cheating! Even Drexler goes to pains to explain that it's "AI *options*, not blind AI optimism. After all, it's a technology some will also use for ill!

But at the very least you probably have (a) models with fewer confusions about what is real and what isn't, what are simulations/evals vs real world (b) less incentive for models to learn that human instructions and developer assurances are routinely misleading (c) a general practice of designing realistic evals and better RL envs, as opposed to contrived setups whose relationship to deployment behaviour is questionable. In fact, I'm surprised there's still so little attention and standards for data quality and eval construct validity.


Kelsey Piper: @ded_ruckus I think we should probably not lie to the AIs in training. This obviously would make our lives harder in the short term but in the long term they get good at telling whether we're lying and we're no better off plus they're all paranoid.

items.title: Does the RBI even need to sterilize the FCNR based inflows? I'm coming to the conclusion the answer is probably no. When RBI creates money by printing...
items.description_html:
Does the RBI even need to sterilize the FCNR based inflows? I'm coming to the conclusion the answer is probably no.

When RBI creates money by printing rupees to buy dollars, the way its done for the FCNR swap, banks have a lot of money with the RBI. The money with the RBI stays with the RBI - it only moves from one bank to the other (or the government).

Whatever banks need for CRR is sequestered away by banks, so the excess liquidity then is placed back into the RBI as reverse repo.

Why would liquidity at the RBI be a problem? If banks were net borrowers from the RBI, then RBI printing has an inflationary impact, perhaps, by reducing borrowing cost due to more supply. That is not the case even before the FCNR, as banks have had excess liquidiyt for a while.

If this excess liquidity causes RBI to pay like 5.25% for it in INR (to banks on reverse repo, that is kinda sorta offset by the 4.4% the RBI earns in dollars for the $127bn reserves they have to keep to return that FCNR. So there's no major impact on RBI accounts.

Will banks go crazy lending? They can't; they will creat NPAs if they go bonkers, and that will destroy their capital. Their capital ratios determine how much their lending can grow. That is not linked with RBI printing money, so banks have net parked excesses with RBI because they don't want to lend beyond capital ratio allowances.

Should the government issue bonds to sterilize, like they did in 2005? No. That time, banks were net borrowers from RBI and inflation was a distinct possibility, so the government did MSS bonds. Not needed now - it moves the interest cost to the govt (deficit increases, inflation increases) but RBI is the one that earns the interest on the USD. Then if people like me say that RBI should pay all those profits back to the government, all the uncles gets full on foaming at the mouth. So let it stay with the RBI (which should anyhow pay any of the profits earned to the govt)

(Note: I first wrote about RBI needing to pay as much as 300,000 cr. as dividends in December 2018. https://premium.capitalmind.in/2018/12/abeyaar-rbi-is-hoarding-too-much-capital-and-can-pay-a-chunk-to-the-government/
After that the govt got paid 1.76 lakh cr as dividends, then after four years of denials, the RBI is now paying more than 2 lakh crores a year to the govt.)

So sterlization isn't necessary and distorts the govt accounts unnecessarily.

items.description_html:
𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚'𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲: 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭'𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚'𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧?

India’s energy transition is no longer just about adding renewable capacity, it is about building an ecosystem that can deliver energy security, reliability and sustainable growth.

At #CareEdgeConversations, industry leaders Mr Kuldeep Jain, Founder & MD, @CleanMax_Ofc; Mr Sandeep Lakhanpal, Managing Director, @JHargrett49946; Mr Kailash Vaswani, CFO, ReNew Energy Global PLCC; and Mr Abishek Pareek, CFO, Waaree Group came together to discuss what lies ahead for India’s energy transition.

Moderated by Sachin Gupta, ED and CRO, CareEdge Ratings, the conversation highlighted some of the critical priorities shaping the next phase:

🔹 Transmission infrastructure needs to keep pace with the rapid addition of renewable capacity.

🔹 Renewables + storage are increasingly becoming commercially competitive with conventional power.

🔹 Supply-chain resilience and backward integration will be critical to India’s energy security.

🔹 Domestic solar manufacturing has significant potential, but scale, technology, and cost competitiveness remain key.

🔹 Capital availability remains strong, particularly for robust projects, while access to debt needs continued attention.

🔹 The C&I renewable energy segment is witnessing rapid growth, opening up significant opportunities for developers.

🔹 Ultimately, India's transition will require an integrated ecosystem spanning generation, transmission, storage, manufacturing, and finance.

The message was clear: India’s renewable journey is entering a more complex but significantly larger phase, one where energy transition and energy security must move together.

items.title: RT محمد عبدالسلام: إن ما قامت به القوات المسلحة اليمنية في بعض المناطق الساحلية عمل...
items.description_html:
RT محمد عبدالسلام
إن ما قامت به القوات المسلحة اليمنية في بعض المناطق الساحلية عملية وطنية في إطار فرض السيادة اليمنية، والتعامل مع التحديات والأطماع التي تهدد السلم الأهلي.
إن السلام الحقيقي والعادل والمشرف كان وسيبقى خيارنا الاستراتيجي، وأن على الجميع أن يدرك بأن خيار السلام مع اليمن هو الأقل كلفة والأقصر طريقا نحو إعادة تنظيم العلاقات وفق مبادئ حسن الجوار والاحترام المتبادل والمصالح المشتركة.
إننا نؤكد أن الجمهورية اليمنية ليست لديها أي مطامع في أي دولة من دول الجوار أو الدول العربية والإسلامية وغيرها من دول العالم، ولم تعتدي على أي دولة بل هي من تم الاعتداء عليها بما يتنافى مع الأخوة الإسلامية والعربية.
أما بشأن حرية الملاحة وحركة التجارة الدولية في البحر الأحمر وباب المندب فهي آمنة ومنتظمة، ولا داعي لأي قلق دولي حيالها، فليس عليها أي خطر من جهة اليمن، والعمليات الجارية حالياً هي محددة الأهداف وفق ما تم الإعلان عنه سابقا وتأتي في الإطار الدفاعي .

items.title: The biggest issue with an AI "safety slowdown:" What happens with China? While there are legitimate concerns around the safety of AI and how quickly i...
items.description_html:
The biggest issue with an AI "safety slowdown:"

What happens with China?

While there are legitimate concerns around the safety of AI and how quickly it is evolving, the AI race is global.

And, in today's ecosystem, falling even 6 months behind in the AI race is like falling decades behind in the pre-AI world.

If US AI giants agree to slow progress and focus on safety, there must be an international agreement in place as well.

And, even if there is an agreement in place, how do we regulate compliance?

We've said it before and we will say it again: AI is the biggest technological revolution in history.

This is an AI arms race that may be impossible to fully regulate.

items.title: China is attempting to refill its oil reserves. Chinese crude imports rose +2.2 million tons in August, to 37.9 million tons, marking their 2nd consec...
items.description_html:
China is attempting to refill its oil reserves.

Chinese crude imports rose +2.2 million tons in August, to 37.9 million tons, marking their 2nd consecutive monthly increase.

This brings the 2-month increase to ~9.0 million tons, or a ~33% recovery from the total drop between January and July this year.

The increase in crude supply has also allowed China to ramp up fuel exports, with overseas sales of gasoline and diesel surging +29% last month.

However, China's crude imports were down -23% year-over-year and -32% below this year's peak.

Meanwhile, China’s massive oil inventories are estimated at more than 1.2 billion barrels, giving the country ample flexibility to reduce purchases as prices rise.

China's massive oil stockpile is growing again.

items.title: The US debt crisis is entering uncharted territory: Net interest, social security, medicare, healthcare spending, and veterans' benefits currently con...
items.description_html:
The US debt crisis is entering uncharted territory:

Net interest, social security, medicare, healthcare spending, and veterans' benefits currently consume 98.4% of total federal government receipts, near the highest proportion on record.

This figure has surged +28 percentage points since 2022 and is only below the 2020 pandemic peak of ~99.0%.

Net interest alone has nearly tripled as a % of revenue, to a record 19.7%, accounting for roughly half of that +28 percentage-point increase.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, these expenditures did not exceed 90% of federal receipts.

In other words, mandatory spending and interest costs now consume nearly every Dollar the federal government collects.

What is the long-term plan here?

items.title: The AI boom is powering historic earnings growth: Full-year S&P 500 profit is now projected to grow +32% YoY in 2026, up from the +24% expected before...
items.description_html:
The AI boom is powering historic earnings growth:

Full-year S&P 500 profit is now projected to grow +32% YoY in 2026, up from the +24% expected before the Q2 earnings season began.

This comes as 86% of S&P 500 companies beat expectations this quarter, the highest beat rate since 2021.

Communication Services saw the largest upward revision, with earnings now expected to grow +51% YoY, nearly double the +26% projected at the start of Q2.

Consumer Discretionary followed, with estimates rising to +32% YoY growth from just +12% previously, driven by Amazon's, $AMZN, results.

Meanwhile, earnings in the energy and information technology sectors are projected to grow +83% and +59% YoY in 2026, respectively.

AI is driving astronomical profit growth.

items.title: Shocking stat of the day: ~$7.0 trillion worth of T-Bills are currently outstanding, with ~$6.1 trillion maturing within the next year. Including the ...
items.description_html:
Shocking stat of the day:

~$7.0 trillion worth of T-Bills are currently outstanding, with ~$6.1 trillion maturing within the next year.

Including the remaining maturities, ~$7.5 trillion worth of marketable Treasury debt is maturing in 2026.

Another ~$4.0 trillion matures in 2027, followed by ~$3.5 trillion in 2028.

Meanwhile, if the Fed hikes rates by 75 basis points, annual interest costs on T-bills alone could rise by ~$50 billion, equivalent to 0.15% of GDP.

This comes as much of this debt would be refinanced at higher market rates than those at which it was originally issued.

The US is set to face a massive refinancing wave at higher borrowing costs.

items.title: BREAKING: Equities now account for a record 48.2% of total US household financial assets. This includes stocks held directly, as well as equities held...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: Equities now account for a record 48.2% of total US household financial assets.

This includes stocks held directly, as well as equities held indirectly through life insurance companies, private pension funds, government retirement funds, and mutual funds.

This figure has risen +13.9 percentage points since the 2022 bear market.

By comparison, at the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble peak, US households held 38.7% of their financial assets in equities.

For perspective, this proportion never exceeded 20% between 1974 and 1992.

Asset owners are winning.

items.title: BREAKING: Earnings for VLCC supertankers on the benchmark Middle East-to-China route are up to nearly $800,000 per day, an all-time high. Rates have m...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: Earnings for VLCC supertankers on the benchmark Middle East-to-China route are up to nearly $800,000 per day, an all-time high.

Rates have more than doubled over the last 2 months.

At the same time, the rate for a VLCC charter from the US Gulf to Asia is up to a record ~$29.5 million per voyage, before additional war-risk costs and fees for potential delays.

The surge has been driven by fewer vessels willing to transit the Strait of Hormuz, sharply reducing available shipping capacity.

As a result, alternative routes keep each tanker at sea for more time, further reducing the number of vessels available.

Looking ahead, earnings for VLCCs are estimated to stay above $100,000 a day into next year, more than double historical levels, which rarely exceeded $45,000 a day, according to Kpler.

Inflation is back.

items.title: Interest costs on global government debt have never been higher: Gross interest expenditure among OECD countries surged +$180 billion YoY in 2025, to ...
items.description_html:
Interest costs on global government debt have never been higher:

Gross interest expenditure among OECD countries surged +$180 billion YoY in 2025, to a record $2.24 trillion.

This marks the 4th consecutive annual increase, totaling +$960 billion.

The US accounted for ~65% of the total, at $1.45 trillion, while the EU represented ~18%, or $400 billion.

As a % of global GDP, gross interest costs stood at ~3.2% last year, their 2nd-highest level in at least 20 years.

Meanwhile, OECD countries are estimated to borrow another $18 trillion in 2026, the highest annual total on record.

The global debt crisis is spiraling out of control.

items.title: BREAKING: The US Debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to rise to a record 156% in 2050, according to the CBO's latest forecast. That would mark a +57 percen...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: The US Debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to rise to a record 156% in 2050, according to the CBO's latest forecast.

That would mark a +57 percentage point increase from the current ~99%.

At the same time, the Treasury Department estimates the ratio will surge to a massive 213% over the same period, or 57 percentage points higher than the CBO's estimate.

Furthermore, neither estimate includes intragovernmental debt, such as Treasury securities held by Social Security and other federal trust funds.

The worst part?

Both forecasts assume the US avoids a recession during this entire period.

US debt could be heading in a far worse direction than forecasts suggest.

items.description_html:
The shift we are seeing right now is extraordinary.

Markets now see a BASE case of 4 interest rate hikes by July 2027.

To put this into perspective, at the start of 2026, markets saw 4 interest rate CUTS during this time period.

That's a difference of +200 basis points between interest rate expectations now and 9 months ago.

These are, by far, the most hawkish Fed policy expectations since the Fed began raising interest rates in March 2022.

It's clear: the market believes "higher for longer" is back and inflation is here to stay.

Wednesday is going to be an eventful day.

items.title: US companies are borrowing at a rapid pace in Europe: US corporates have raised €149 billion, or $173 billion, in European bonds so far in 2026, the ...
items.description_html:
US companies are borrowing at a rapid pace in Europe:

US corporates have raised €149 billion, or $173 billion, in European bonds so far in 2026, the 2nd-highest annual total on record.

This is also double the full-year amount seen in 2022 and 2023.

At this pace, US firms are set to borrow a record €225 billion, or $261 billion, this year.

This comes as heavy AI-related borrowing from Big Tech has crowded the US Dollar bond market, leaving other issuers facing worse pricing and less room to raise debt domestically.

Euro-denominated debt is also cheaper to service for high-grade borrowers than US Dollar debt, a key advantage for global companies earning revenue in Euros.

US firms are increasingly looking abroad for financing as the US market can no longer easily absorb the debt wave.

items.title: US housing affordability is rapidly deteriorating: The annual income needed to afford an average home in the US surged +$4,107 in May, to a record $12...
items.description_html:
US housing affordability is rapidly deteriorating:

The annual income needed to afford an average home in the US surged +$4,107 in May, to a record $124,674 per year.

This marks the 3rd consecutive monthly increase, totaling +$9,734.

By comparison, US median household income stands at $86,159 per year.

This brings the gap between median household income and the income needed to afford an average home to $38,515, the largest gap since July 2025.

This is just $2,288 below the $40,803 record set in June 2024.

To put this into perspective, median household income was $5,139 higher than the income required to buy a home in 2021.

Homeownership is becoming increasingly out of reach for the average American.

This also follows +$190 billion in total inflows in July and +$220 billion in June.

In the first 8 months of 2026, US ETFs have seen +$1.4 trillion in inflows, on track for their largest annual intake on record.

Equity funds accounted for ~63%, or +$880 billion, of the total.

Investor risk appetite remains incredibly strong.

items.description_html:
Leveraged funds are becoming increasingly bearish on US tech:

Leveraged fund short positions on Nasdaq 100 futures are up to ~$75 billion, near their highest in at least 4 years.

Short positioning has more than doubled since February.

Meanwhile, long positioning on Nasdaq 100 futures is down to ~$18 billion, its lowest since mid-2025.

As a result, net positioning among leveraged funds is down to -$57 billion, near its lowest since at least 2022.

This marks a sharp reversal from the positive net positioning recorded in November 2025.

Leveraged funds are increasingly betting against tech stocks.

items.title: The BRICS Summit headlines so far ! 1. Iran & UAE agreed to the same language on the Middle East war. Iran is a BRICS member while UAE is closely alig...
items.description_html:
The BRICS Summit headlines so far !

1. Iran & UAE agreed to the same language on the Middle East war. Iran is a BRICS member while UAE is closely aligned with the U.S. - so this is significant.

2. BRICS took a position clearly uncomfortable for the U.S. - the declaration criticises unilateral sanctions & tariff/non-tariff measures.. Basically says sanctions outside the UN framework should be eliminated.

3. India has tried to prevent BRICS becoming an anti-West bloc. PM Modi's formulation - "BRICS is not against anyone". This kind of also points to a more fundamental tension within the bloc - Russia & China are much more comfortable presenting it as a counterweight to Western power. India & Brazil not so much.

4. President Xi is in India for the first time in 7 years. PM Modi reiterated that peace on the border remains the essential basis for a normal relationship. The Modi-Xi bilateral may ultimately matter a lot.

5. Xi is trying to position China & BRICS as a peacemaker in the Iran conflict. He explicitly urged BRICS countries to play a peace-making role and said China was prepared to do its part.

6. President Putin has used the summit to reinforce the Russia-India relationship & his wider argument that Russia is not isolated. In his bilateral with Modi, the two reiterated the target of taking bilateral trade towards $100 billion by 2030.

7. There has been a significant absence - no dramatic 'BRICS currency' moment. This is worth stressing because headlines around BRICS often overstate de-dollarization.

items.title: RT ValueEquity: For me at least, position sizing is not directly correlated to highest conviction idea , it is a mix of lowest valuation and moderate ...
items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
For me at least, position sizing is not directly correlated to highest conviction idea , it is a mix of lowest valuation and moderate conviction that builds a large position sizing

Margin of safety + conviction would mean a larger allocation Do not confuse conviction and allocation and ego , let market decide the allocation by the gains making the stock a large part of your portfolio Your view has to be rewarded by the market to make it a larger size and then see how the thesis is evolving , I don't want to put my ego and allocate 10% to a stock and hope that it plays out , I don't consider myself that smart

I only go that aggressive when I see great valuations for a great business with incremental delta in earnings is clearly mapped out through capacity or platform business type growth mapping , went aggressive with Laurus in 2023 , car trade last year and got rewarded big time

Ather Energy: Building A Scalable EV Platform Beyond Premium Scooters

Ather is transitioning from a premium electric scooter maker into a broader EV mobility platform by expanding its product portfolio, manufacturing capacity, distribution network and software ecosystem.

Key Strategic Progress

1. Product Portfolio Expansion

Expanded beyond the core 450 platform with Rizta S (159 km) and Rizta S (161 km) variants.
Rizta has become Ather’s fastest-selling product, strengthening its presence in the family scooter segment.
Upcoming EL platform and e-bike portfolio could expand its addressable market beyond scooters.

2. Geographic Expansion

Replicated its South India success model in new markets.
Middle India market share increased from 4.1% in Q1 FY25 to 17.4% in Q4 FY26.
The company is now scaling this playbook across the rest of India through stronger retail and service presence.

3. Distribution & Service Network Scale-Up

Retail and service network doubled during FY26.
Wider footprint improves customer accessibility and supports faster adoption in new regions.

4. Manufacturing Scale-Up

Factory 3.0 development is progressing, with Phase 1 targeting 5 lakh units annual capacity.
Upon completion of both phases, combined manufacturing capacity across Hosur and Factory 3.0 is expected to reach 14.2 lakh units annually.
Increased localisation of components like transmission, electronics and painting can improve cost efficiency and supply-chain resilience.

5. Software-Led Revenue Opportunity

AtherStack Pro achieved 91% attach rate in FY26.
Software and digital services are becoming an additional revenue stream, improving customer lifetime value.

6. Margin Improvement & Operating Leverage

Gross margin, EBITDA margin and profitability improved through:
Higher operating leverage
Better cost discipline
Scale benefits

Investment Perspective
Ather’s next phase is not just about selling more scooters — it is about building a vertically integrated EV ecosystem.

The key factors to track:

EL platform adoption

Factory 3.0 ramp-up

Expansion beyond South India

Improvement in margins

Growth of software-led revenues

If execution remains strong, Ather could evolve from a niche premium EV player into a scaled EV technology company with multiple growth engines.

items.title: Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather t...
items.description_html:
Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products

Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather than conventional textile demand. The company manufactures specialised yarns engineered for specific performance characteristics such as high tensile strength, flame resistance, heat resistance, chemical stability, abrasion resistance and anti-static properties.

Its products ultimately find applications across defence, protective clothing, automotive components, filtration and pollution control, geotextiles, industrial fabrics, thermal insulation, packaging and home furnishing.

Why the Business Looks Interesting

1. The biggest change is happening in the revenue mix and profitability.

Revenue from operations increased only modestly from Rs. 109.9 crore in FY24 to Rs. 117.4 crore in FY26, but EBITDA increased from Rs. 16.1 crore to Rs. 31.1 crore over the same period.

As a result:

EBITDA margin: 14.7% → 15.6% → 26.5%
PAT: Rs. 7.0 crore → Rs. 8.5 crore → Rs. 16.0 crore
PAT margin: 6.4% → 7.5% → 13.7%
ROCE: 21.0% → 16.3% → 26.3%

So FY26 growth was less about topline acceleration and more about a sharp improvement in business mix and profitability.

The most interesting development is the shift away from Indutech towards higher-growth categories.

2. What Industries Does It Serve?

Its yarn portfolio gives it exposure to several specialised applications:

Protech: Flame-retardant and heat-resistant yarns used in PPE, safety apparel and industrial thermal barriers.

Mobiltech: Friction-resistant yarns used in brake pads, clutch facings and transmission components.

Indutech: Filtration, filter cartridges, ropes, webbings and other industrial applications.

Hometech: Home furnishing textiles, carpets and filtration media.

Its broader product range includes para-aramid-based spun yarn, high-tenacity polyester, meta-aramid, FR viscose, modacrylic yarn, polypropylene yarn, stainless-steel yarn and specialised friction-spun yarns.
That creates exposure to structural themes including industrial safety, defence, automotive, pollution control and filtration, infrastructure and specialised manufacturing.

3. Capacity Is Becoming The Next Constraint

The company's main technical/synthetic yarn capacity stood at 3,750 MT in FY26, while production reached 3,619 MT.

That means utilisation has increased sharply:

FY24: 80.2%
FY25: 86.6%
FY26: 96.5%

This is important because the existing facility is approaching full utilisation precisely when newer categories such as Protech are scaling.

Ashutosh Fibre therefore plans to expand within its existing Petlad, Gujarat facility, adding compact spinning systems and high-value yarn attachments such as the Pinter Hard Core system.

Expanding within the existing facility should allow the company to leverage existing infrastructure, workforce and administrative resources — potentially making the expansion more capital-efficient.
Moving Downstream Into Modacrylic Fabrics
Another interesting strategy is forward integration.

4. Moving up in Value Chain
Ashutosh already manufactures modacrylic-based yarn used for high-performance fabrics. It now wants to move into manufacturing and selling the fabric itself.

The company has started trial production through third-party weaving and processing facilities and is targeting approximately 20,000 metres of modacrylic-based fabric sales per month.

The important part is that Ashutosh's own yarn would be consumed as the raw material.

This potentially allows it to move from being only a yarn supplier towards a higher-value finished technical textile product, improving value addition and potentially margins.

5. Exports Could Become Another Growth Lever

Exports are already meaningful:

FY24: Rs. 47.9 crore — 43.6% of revenue
FY25: Rs. 43.4 crore — 38.1%
FY26: Rs. 45.8 crore — 39.0%

The company plans to use additional capacity to target new international markets for specialised technical yarns.

Ashutosh Fibre is interesting because three transitions are happening simultaneously:

Volume → Value: Higher-value technical and performance yarns are becoming more important.

Yarn → Fabric: The company is attempting to move downstream into modacrylic technical fabrics.

Domestic + Existing Exports → Larger Global Opportunity: Nearly 40% of revenue already comes from exports, while new capacity is intended partly to deepen international penetration.

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.title: 🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns: 1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Ris...
items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https:/...
items.description_html:
A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https://vro.in/s229348. The line came from Vineet Nayar's new book, Humans First, Machines Second. His point is plain. AI is powerful and everyone has it. Something everyone has cannot make anyone special.
That left a question I did not answer. If the machine is common, what is uncommon?
I think the machine has taken the middle of the work and left us the two ends. It has not taken the beginning, which is deciding what question to ask. It has not taken the end, which is deciding whether the answer is any good.
Ask an AI to analyse a fund and you will get a competent analysis of that fund. It will not tell you that the reader's real problem is not this fund but whether he should be in this category at all. Knowing that comes from thirty years of reading letters from investors.
The machine will also give you ten sensible options. Picking the one that suits this reader in this market is not calculation. It is judgement, and judgement is mostly the memory of having been wrong before.
Then there is the story. The investor who sold everything in March 2020 did not lack information. He lacked a story strong enough to hold him when the fear came. Nobody gets that story from a prompt. AI can help you invent. It cannot invent.
One more thing. The machine agrees with you. Tell it you like a stock and it will find reasons to like it. What a person needs from an advisor or an editor is the opposite: someone willing to say no.
Nayar says the danger is not smarter machines but people losing faith in what only they can do. In our business, that is the risk worth worrying about.

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

RT Aaron Levie
Good post. Don’t agree with all of it, but it represents many of the actual practical realities for the general path forward in frontier AI whether we like it or not.

At the level of capability we’re seeing from models there will inevitably be some form of coordinated self-regulation of the industry; that’s generally a good thing. The big question will be if everyone can agree to what that is. However, the way things are headed politically there’s a chance that the labs won’t even get a say in it.

And then the bigger question yet is do all the countries participate or not. Any “slow down” hinges on broad participation, which from a game theory standpoint isn’t likely until the risks are more severe and obvious.

Expect this to be pretty messy for a while.

items.description_html:
India’s retail stockbroking industry has a profit pool of more than $1 billion, or roughly Rs 10,000 crore.

It has produced some of the most profitable companies in India’s internet ecosystem.

Zerodha and, more recently, Groww have generated net margins of 45–50%.

Investors and entrepreneurs continue to see an opportunity to capture a share of this profit pool.

Zerodha established its dominance by entering discount broking early. It remains the country’s largest stockbroking platform by revenue and profit.

Groww began as a mutual fund distributor before expanding rapidly into stocks. It is now India’s largest broker by active users.

The next battle, however, may not be for every investor. It is increasingly for the most active and valuable traders on these platforms.

Dhan has already become a unicorn by focusing on this segment.

The latest challenger is Sahi, founded by former Amazon executive and Swiggy CTO Dale Vaz.

Over the past few months, Sahi has emerged as one of the fastest growing brokers in terms of new user additions, even though its base remains much smaller compared to incumbents.

@PratikBhakta_89 has more on its strategy - https://www.thearcweb.com/article/sahi-dale-vaz-stocks-groww-zerodha-JvhwMSEL0109eyoX

items.title: NPCI, which operates UPI, saw its consolidated operating revenue grow 22% to Rs 4,240 crore in FY26. However, its net surplus, or profit, fell 32% to ...
items.description_html:
NPCI, which operates UPI, saw its consolidated operating revenue grow 22% to Rs 4,240 crore in FY26.

However, its net surplus, or profit, fell 32% to Rs 989 crore.

The main reason for the decline was not operating expenses but tax, which nearly tripled to Rs 899 crore.

Deferred tax was the biggest swing, moving from a credit of Rs 11 crore in FY25 to an expense of Rs 331 crore in FY26.

Surplus before tax, meanwhile, increased 5% to Rs 1,888 crore.

Marketing alone accounted for nearly half of NPCI’s total expenses as it continued spending on RuPay incentives, cashback and digital-payment adoption.

Marketing spending increased 27% to Rs 1,420 crore, while employee expenses grew 23% to Rs 534 crore.

items.title: RT Antonio García Martínez (agm.eth): Theory: The difference in AI doomerism is largely generational, with the youngs thinking it's the end of the w...
items.description_html:
RT Antonio García Martínez (agm.eth)
Theory: The difference in AI doomerism is largely generational, with the youngs thinking it's the end of the world and the olds not. Note how the 20-something lab staff thinks it's the techno-Rapture, and everyone from Jensen to pmarca (the olds) are telling them to chill out.

This is a symptom of a larger trend I've noticed as someone in the Xennial generation increasingly surrounded by Zoomers. There's what I call The Great Generational Inversion. The standard trope is that the conservative olds are scandalized by wayward youth, but it's precisely the opposite now.

The youngs don't offend me; I'd scandalize them if I actually said what I think. I'm not trying to censor them, they're (literally in my case, cf. Chaos Monkeys) trying to censor me. They don't seem wild and devil-may-care to me, they seem cautious and anxious and conformist. I'm still riding to hell on a fast horse lifestyle-wise, and they're all popping pills and peptides and as obsessed with their health as hypochondriac grandmas. The things the youth could always be depended on to do to excess--drinking, driving, fornication--they increasingly don't do at all.

It's very strange. Again, you could discard all this as the prattling of an out-of-touch boomer...but I'm not whining about our wanton, irresponsible youth, I'm saying they remind me of my grandparents and wish they lived a little more. It isn't how it's supposed to be, which makes it all the stranger.

Wonder if the generations will just all be flipped from the historical pattern going forward, or if this is a post-COVID one-off.

🚨 Meesho has discontinued the role of chief product officer as part of a restructuring of its product organisation.

Product leaders who previously reported to CPO Prasanna Arunachalam will now report directly to their respective business heads.

Meesho said the change is intended to "strengthen accountability" and align "product strategy and execution with the long term needs of each business."

Arunachalam will no longer be classified as senior management personnel, although he will remain at the company.

Arunachalam was elevated to CPO in June 2025 after nearly five years at Meesho, where he previously led monetisation and content commerce.

He has about about 15 years of work experience at cos like online travel platform Cleartrip, advertising-tech company Vizury and Procter & Gamble.
